collection_intro: Short, ungraded practice checks, one for each section of Chapter 9 of *Java Programming*, 10th edition. Rate your confidence, answer, and read the feedback: the review at the end points you to exactly what to re-read.

checks.title: Learning About the Concept of Inheritance
checks.subtitle: Base and derived classes, the is-a test, and how inheritance differs from composition and aggregation
checks.intro: A payroll system already has a tested `Employee` class, and now the company hires salespeople who also need a territory. Four questions on reusing what already works.
takeaways: Inheritance lets a new class acquire every field and method of an existing class, so you write only what is different. It adds no new power; it saves time and reuses code that is already tested.
Use the is-a test to find the base class: a derived class is always a more specific case of its base class (an `Evergreen` is a `Tree`), never the other way around.
"Has-a" is containment, not inheritance. In composition the contained objects stop existing with their container; in aggregation they continue to exist on their own.

questions.concept: The is-a test identifies inheritance
questions.stem: Which pair of classes is best modeled with inheritance, the first class extending the second?

options.text: `Evergreen` and `Tree`
options.feedback: "An Evergreen is a Tree" is true, and "a Tree is an Evergreen" is not. That one-way is-a relationship is exactly what inheritance models.

options.text: `Department` and `Business`
options.feedback: A business *has* departments; a department is not a kind of business. That is containment (composition), not inheritance.

options.text: `Employee` and `Department`
options.feedback: A department *has* employees, and an employee is not a kind of department. That relationship is aggregation.

options.text: `Tree` and `Evergreen`
options.feedback: This reverses the direction. Not every tree is an evergreen, so `Tree` is the more general base class.

questions.hint: Say each pair as a sentence: "A ___ is a ___." Which sentence is true for every object of the first class?
questions.explanation: A derived class is always a more specific case of its base class, so "Derived is a Base" must be true for every derived object. When the honest sentence is "A has a B", the relationship is containment, not inheritance.
questions.aside: Experienced designers often reach for has-a first. The 1994 book *Design Patterns* (the "Gang of Four") advises "favor object composition over class inheritance", because a contained object can be swapped out later and an inherited parent cannot.

questions.concept: Composition versus aggregation
questions.stem: A `Business` contains `Department` objects, and each `Department` contains `Employee` objects. If the business closes, its departments disappear, but the employees still exist. How do the two relationships differ?

options.text: Business–Department is composition; Department–Employee is aggregation
options.feedback: Departments don't outlive the business that contains them (composition); employees do outlive their department (aggregation).

options.text: Business–Department is aggregation; Department–Employee is composition
options.feedback: This swaps the definitions. The relationship where the parts die with the whole is composition.

options.text: Both are inheritance, because each class holds objects of the other
options.feedback: Holding objects is has-a, not is-a. A department is not a kind of business, and an employee is not a kind of department.

options.text: Both are composition, because each class contains an array of members
options.feedback: Containing members is true of both, but composition also means the members can't exist without the container. Employees can.

questions.hint: For each pair, ask what happens to the contained objects when their container goes away.
questions.explanation: Both composition and aggregation are has-a containment. They differ in lifetime: composed parts exist only as part of their container, while aggregated parts continue to exist without it.

questions.concept: A subclass contains everything its superclass has
questions.stem: The `EmployeeWithTerritory` class file declares only one field and two methods; `Employee` declares two fields and four methods. Which statement about an `EmployeeWithTerritory` object is accurate?

options.text: It has three fields and six methods: its own plus all of `Employee`'s
options.feedback: A subclass contains every field and method of its superclass as well as the ones it adds, so its objects are usually larger than the parent's.

options.text: It has one field and two methods, because only those appear in its file
options.feedback: A short class file can be misleading. Writing `extends Employee` brings in everything declared in `Employee`.

options.text: It has two fields and four methods, because the parent's members replace its own
options.feedback: Nothing is replaced: the subclass keeps the parent's members and adds its own on top.

options.text: It has the parent's methods but none of its fields, which stay in `Employee`
options.feedback: Fields are inherited too. Every `EmployeeWithTerritory` object holds an `id` and a `salary`, even though it can't reach them directly while they are private.

questions.hint: When you say "extends Employee", what comes along with the new class?
questions.explanation: A subclass description can look small, but every subclass object contains all of its superclass's fields and methods plus the new, more specific ones. That is why a subclass is usually larger than its superclass.

questions.concept: What inheritance does and doesn't give you
questions.stem: A classmate says, "Inheritance lets Java programs do things that would be impossible without it." Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Nothing new becomes possible; it saves time and reuses tested code
options.feedback: Without inheritance you could still write every class from scratch. Inheritance makes the job faster and less error-prone.

options.text: It's right, because a subclass can reach its parent's private data
options.feedback: Private members are exactly what a subclass *can't* reach directly. Inheritance respects information hiding.

options.text: It's right, because inherited methods run faster than rewritten ones
options.feedback: Inherited methods are not faster. The gain is in programmer time and fewer errors, not execution speed.

options.text: Nothing is gained at all; copying the code by hand is equally safe
options.feedback: Copied code must be retested and maintained in two places. Reusing tested methods is exactly what reduces errors.

questions.hint: Could you write `EmployeeWithTerritory` if Java had no `extends` keyword? What would it cost you?
questions.explanation: Inheritance does not give you the ability to write programs you could not write otherwise. It saves time because fields and methods already exist, reduces errors because they are already tested, and reduces learning for programmers who know the parent class.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.1, Learning About the Concept of Inheritance (pp. 330–331)

checks.title: Extending Classes
checks.subtitle: The extends keyword, what a subclass object can call, the one-way direction of inheritance, and instanceof
checks.intro: A party planner already has a `Party` class, and now some parties serve dinner. Five questions on what one word, `extends`, gives a new class.
takeaways: `class Child extends Parent` gives every `Child` object the parent's fields and nonprivate methods; the child adds only what is new.
Inheritance is one-way. A parent object can't call methods that only a child declares, because the parent knows nothing about the subclasses that might be written later.
`obj instanceof SomeClass` is `true` when `obj` is a `SomeClass` or any descendant of it, so a child object is an instance of its parent's class as well as its own.

questions.concept: The extends keyword
questions.stem: Which class header makes `EmployeeWithTerritory` a subclass of `Employee` in Java?

options.text: `public class EmployeeWithTerritory extends Employee`
options.feedback: `extends` names the one superclass, and the new class receives its fields and methods.

options.text: `public class EmployeeWithTerritory inherits Employee`
options.feedback: "Inherits" describes what happens, but it isn't a Java keyword. The header would not compile.

options.text: `public class EmployeeWithTerritory : Employee`
options.feedback: The colon is how C# and C++ write inheritance. Java spells the relationship out with a keyword.

options.text: `public class Employee extends EmployeeWithTerritory`
options.feedback: This makes `Employee` the child. The more specific class is the one that extends the general one.

questions.hint: Which keyword says the new class *adds to* an existing one?
questions.explanation: In Java, a subclass names its superclass after the keyword `extends` in its class header. The subclass automatically receives the superclass's data fields and methods and then adds its own.

questions.concept: A subclass object can call inherited methods
questions.stem: `DinnerParty` declares no `setGuests()` or `getGuests()`. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `12 guests, menu 2`
options.feedback: `setGuests()` and `getGuests()` come from `Party`, so the `DinnerParty` object stores and returns its guest count through them.

options.text: `0 guests, menu 2`
options.feedback: This assumes the inherited method sets a different object's field. The `guests` field set here belongs to `aDinnerParty` itself.

options.text: It does not compile, because `DinnerParty` has no `setGuests()` method
options.feedback: `DinnerParty` doesn't *declare* one, but it inherits one from `Party`. Inherited methods are callable as if written in the child.

options.text: It does not compile, because `guests` is private in `Party`
options.feedback: The code never touches `guests` directly; it uses the public `setGuests()` and `getGuests()`, which can reach the private field.

questions.hint: Where does `aDinnerParty` find a method it doesn't declare?
questions.explanation: A subclass object can call every nonprivate method of its superclass as if the subclass had declared it. Those methods work on the subclass object's own copy of the inherited fields.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.2, You Do It: Creating an Application That Uses the DinnerParty Class (pp. 335–336)

questions.concept: Inheritance is one-way
questions.stem: What happens when this code is compiled?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error at `clerk.setTerritory(5)`: `Employee` has no such method
options.feedback: Only the child declares `setTerritory()`. The compiler looks at `Employee` and finds no such method.

options.text: It compiles and runs; `clerk` simply ignores the territory
options.feedback: Java doesn't silently ignore calls. A method the type doesn't have is a compile-time error.

options.text: It compiles, then throws an exception when `setTerritory()` runs
options.feedback: The compiler catches this before the program ever runs, because it knows `Employee` declares no `setTerritory()`.

options.text: It compiles and works, because every class can use its subclasses' methods
options.feedback: That's the reverse of inheritance. A child gets the parent's methods; a parent never gets a child's.

questions.hint: Which class declares `setTerritory()`, and which class is `clerk`?
questions.explanation: Inheritance is a one-way proposition: a child inherits from its parent, not the other way around. A parent class object has no access to methods that only a subclass declares.

questions.concept: Why a parent can't use a child's members
questions.stem: An `Orthodontist` object can call `Dentist`'s `billPatients()`. Why does calling `Orthodontist`'s `applyBraces()` on a plain `Dentist` object fail to compile?

options.text: `Dentist` is written before its subclasses and can't know what they'll add
options.feedback: A parent is written first and can have any number of later children. It can't promise methods that only some future child will add.

options.text: Methods declared in a subclass are private unless marked otherwise
options.feedback: `applyBraces()` can be public and the rule still holds. The limit comes from the direction of inheritance, not access.

options.text: Java copies methods only from the newer class to the older class
options.feedback: Methods flow from parent to child, and the parent is usually the older class. This has the direction reversed.

options.text: A `Dentist` object is too small in memory to hold the child's methods
options.feedback: Memory size isn't the reason. A plain `Dentist` simply isn't an `Orthodontist`, so it has no braces to apply.

questions.hint: Which class has to exist first, and how much can it know about the classes that extend it?
questions.explanation: Subclasses are more specific than the superclass they extend. Every child is a parent, so it gets the parent's general methods, but a parent object is not any particular child, so it can't use a child's specialized methods.

questions.concept: instanceof is true for the class and its ancestors
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `true true false`
options.feedback: `northernRep` is an `EmployeeWithTerritory` and therefore also an `Employee`. A plain `Employee` is not an `EmployeeWithTerritory`.

options.text: `true false false`
options.feedback: This treats `instanceof` as an exact-class test. It is also true for every ancestor of the object's class.

options.text: `true true true`
options.feedback: This runs the relationship both ways. A parent object is not an instance of its child class.

options.text: `false true false`
options.feedback: An object is always an instance of the class that created it, so the first test must be true.

questions.hint: Can the object on the left be treated as the type on the right?
questions.explanation: `instanceof` yields `true` when the object on its left can be upcast to the type on its right: its own class or any superclass. A superclass object is not an instance of its subclasses.
questions.aside: Since Java 16, `instanceof` can also declare a variable: `if (obj instanceof Employee e)` tests the object and, when the test passes, gives you `e` already typed as an `Employee`, with no separate cast.

checks.title: Overriding Superclass Methods
checks.subtitle: Overriding versus overloading, polymorphism, return types, and the @Override annotation
checks.intro: Hourly workers are paid per hour and contractors per contract, yet every paycheck screen calls one method: `displayRateOfPay()`. Five questions on giving one name many behaviors.
takeaways: A subclass method overrides a superclass method only when it has the same name and the same parameter list. With the same name but different parameters, it overloads instead, and the object has both versions.
When a method is overridden, calling it on a subclass object runs the subclass version. Using one name for different implementations is polymorphism.
`@Override` tells the compiler you mean to override, so a misspelled name or wrong parameter list becomes a compile error instead of a silent new method.

questions.concept: The child's version runs for a child object
questions.stem: `DinnerParty2` overrides `displayInvitation()`. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `party! dinner party!`
options.feedback: Each object runs the version its own class provides: `Party`'s for the `Party`, the overriding one for the `DinnerParty2`.

options.text: `party! party!`
options.feedback: That would be true if `DinnerParty2` only inherited the method. Because it declares the same signature, its own version replaces the parent's for its objects.

options.text: `party! dinner party! party!`
options.feedback: Overriding replaces the parent's version for the child object; Java doesn't run both unless the child calls `super.displayInvitation()`.

options.text: `dinner party! dinner party!`
options.feedback: Overriding changes the behavior of child objects only. A plain `Party` object still uses `Party`'s method.

questions.hint: Which class created each object, and does that class declare its own `displayInvitation()`?
questions.explanation: When a child class declares a method with the same name and parameter list as a parent method, it overrides the parent's version. Calling the method on a child object runs the child's version; parent objects are unaffected.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.3, You Do It: Overriding a Superclass Method (pp. 338–339)

questions.concept: Different parameters overload rather than override
questions.stem: `HourlyEmployee` adds a `displayRateOfPay(int hours)` method. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `per week per hour`
options.feedback: The child's method has a different parameter list, so it overloads rather than overrides. The no-argument call still finds `Employee`'s version.

options.text: `per hour per hour`
options.feedback: This assumes the child's method replaced the parent's. It can't: replacing needs the same parameter list, and these lists differ.

options.text: `per week per week`
options.feedback: The call with an argument matches only the `int` version, which the child declares, so the second word is `per hour`.

options.text: It does not compile: a class can't have two methods with one name
options.feedback: Two methods with the same name and different parameter lists are legal overloads. The object has access to both.

questions.hint: Compare the two parameter lists. Does the child's method replace the parent's, or sit beside it?
questions.explanation: A subclass method overrides a superclass method only if both the name and the parameter list match. With a different parameter list, the subclass method overloads the inherited one, and a subclass object can call either version.

questions.concept: @Override catches a mistyped header
questions.stem: A student overrides `displayInvitation()` but types a lowercase *i*. What happens when `DinnerParty2` is compiled?

code.label: Java

error_contains: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype

options.text: A compile error: the method doesn't override anything in `Party`
options.feedback: `@Override` promises an override. `displayinvitation()` matches no parent method, so the compiler reports the broken promise.

options.text: It compiles and overrides, because Java ignores case in method names
options.feedback: Java is case-sensitive: `displayinvitation` and `displayInvitation` are two different identifiers.

options.text: It compiles and adds a new method; `@Override` is only a comment
options.feedback: That would be the result *without* the annotation. With it, the compiler checks your intent and stops.

options.text: It compiles, then fails when a `DinnerParty2` object calls the method
options.feedback: Annotation checks happen at compile time. The class never gets far enough to run.

questions.hint: What does `@Override` ask the compiler to confirm about the method below it?
questions.explanation: `@Override` announces that a method is meant to override a superclass method, and the compiler reports an error if it doesn't. Without the annotation, a typo silently creates a new, unrelated method, and the parent's version keeps running.
questions.aside: Annotations such as `@Override` arrived in Java 5 in 2004. Before then, a misspelled "override" compiled silently, and the only symptom was the parent's version running at the wrong moment.

questions.concept: Return types must be compatible
questions.stem: The child keeps the name and the (empty) parameter list but changes the return type. What happens when this compiles?

code.label: Java

error_contains: return type double is not compatible with int

options.text: A compile error: `double` is not compatible with the inherited `int`
options.feedback: Same name and parameters means this method *would* override `getValue()`. An overriding method can't change the result to an incompatible type, so the compiler refuses.

options.text: It compiles, and the child's version overloads the parent's `getValue()`
options.feedback: Overloading needs a different parameter list. Return type alone can't tell two methods apart, because a call doesn't mention it.

options.text: It compiles; the child's version overrides it and returns `double`
options.feedback: The signature matches, so this is an override attempt, but Java won't let an override return an incompatible type.

options.text: It compiles; each class keeps its own version for its own objects
options.feedback: A child can't have a second method with the parent's exact signature. With matching signatures there is one method slot, and its type must fit.

questions.hint: Which two things decide whether a child method overrides a parent method, and what does a call like `obj.getValue()` not mention?
questions.explanation: Overriding is decided by the method's name and parameter list (its signature), not by its return type. Once the signatures match, the child's return type must be compatible with the parent's, so changing it to an unrelated type is a compile error.

questions.concept: Subtype polymorphism
questions.stem: Polymorphism means one name with many forms. Which example is the *subtype* polymorphism that this section builds with inheritance?

options.text: `Guitar` and `Drum` each override `MusicalInstrument`'s `play()`
options.feedback: Subclasses of one parent each give the same inherited method their own implementation. That is subtype polymorphism.

options.text: The `+` operator adds two `int`s but joins two `String`s together
options.feedback: `+` is polymorphic, but it works by operand type, with no superclass or subclass involved.

options.text: One class declares both `setPay(double)` and `setPay(double, int)`
options.feedback: Overloads are polymorphic too, but the call is chosen by its arguments, not by a subclass's version of an inherited method.

options.text: A local variable named `rate` hides a field named `rate`
options.feedback: That reuse of a name is about scope. No method is given different implementations.

questions.hint: Which example needs a superclass and subclasses to exist?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism is any use of one name for different behaviors. When subclasses of the same parent each implement an inherited method in their own way, Java developers call it subtype polymorphism, and it is a basic requirement for a language to be considered object-oriented.

checks.title: Calling Constructors During Inheritance
checks.subtitle: Constructor order, superclass constructors that need arguments, and super(...)
checks.intro: A subclass that compiled yesterday fails today, and the only change was a new constructor in its *parent*. Five questions on how objects are built in layers.
takeaways: Creating a subclass object runs the superclass constructor first, then the subclass constructor, all the way down the chain, even though only one object is created.

If you write no call, Java inserts `super()` with no arguments. So when a superclass has only constructors that need arguments, every subclass must write a constructor that calls `super(...)` with them.
A subclass constructor's parameter list doesn't have to match its parent's: it only has to pass the parent constructor what it needs, using the keyword `super`, never the parent's class name.

questions.concept: Superclass constructors run first
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Party Dinner Wedding`
options.feedback: Before each constructor's own statements run, it calls its parent's. The chain starts at the top, so `Party` prints first.

options.text: `Wedding Dinner Party`
options.feedback: This reads the chain from the object you named upward. Construction runs the other way: the most general part is built first.

options.text: `Wedding`
options.feedback: Only one object is created, but three constructors run. Each ancestor's constructor builds its part of the object.

options.text: `Dinner Wedding`
options.feedback: The chain doesn't stop at the direct parent. `DinnerParty`'s constructor also calls `Party`'s before its own body runs.

questions.hint: Before any constructor's body runs, what must happen to the part of the object it inherits?
questions.explanation: When you create a subclass object, the superclass constructor must execute first, then the subclass constructor. With several generations, constructors run from the most general ancestor down to the class you instantiated.

questions.concept: A superclass that needs arguments forces a subclass constructor
questions.stem: The only `PartyWithConstructor2` constructor now requires an `int`. Why does the subclass, unchanged, stop compiling?

code.label: Java

error_contains: cannot be applied to given types

options.text: Its automatic constructor calls a no-argument `super()` that no longer exists
options.feedback: Without a constructor of its own, the subclass gets a default one that calls the parent's no-argument constructor. The parent no longer has one.

options.text: A subclass must redeclare the `guests` field that the parent's constructor sets
options.feedback: The subclass already inherits `guests`. Redeclaring it wouldn't fix the missing constructor call.

options.text: No subclass can compile unless it declares at least one constructor of its own
options.feedback: The subclass compiled fine before the parent changed. A subclass needs its own constructor only in this situation.

options.text: It still compiles; Java passes 0 for the missing `numGuests` argument
options.feedback: Java never invents arguments. With no `int` to pass, the call to the parent's constructor fails to compile.

questions.hint: If you write no constructor, what does Java's automatic constructor call first?
questions.explanation: A class with no constructor gets a default one, and every constructor that doesn't call `super(...)` explicitly begins with an implicit `super()`. When the superclass has only constructors that need arguments, the subclass must write a constructor that calls one of them.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.4, Inheritance When the Superclass Requires Constructor Arguments (p. 343)

questions.concept: Calling a superclass constructor with super
questions.stem: `Employee`'s only constructor is `Employee(char dept, double rate, int hours)`. Which `HourlyEmployee` constructor compiles?

options.text: `public HourlyEmployee() { super('P', 22.35, 40); }`
options.feedback: The subclass needs no parameters of its own; it just has to hand the parent constructor the three values it requires.

options.text: `public HourlyEmployee() { Employee('P', 22.35, 40); }`
options.feedback: It seems natural to call the parent constructor by name, but Java doesn't allow it. The call must use the keyword `super`.

options.text: `public HourlyEmployee() { this('P', 22.35, 40); }`
options.feedback: `this(...)` calls another constructor of `HourlyEmployee` itself, and it has none with these parameters. The parent is reached with `super`.

options.text: `public HourlyEmployee() { }`
options.feedback: An empty body still begins with an implicit `super()`, and `Employee` has no constructor without parameters.

questions.hint: What does `Employee`'s only constructor need, and what keyword reaches it from a subclass?
questions.explanation: A subclass calls a superclass constructor with `super(arguments)`, and the arguments must match a superclass constructor. They can come from the subclass constructor's parameters or be constants.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.4, Using Superclass Constructors That Require Arguments (p. 341)

questions.concept: A default superclass constructor removes the requirement
questions.stem: `Party` has two constructors, and `DinnerParty` declares none. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `default`
options.feedback: With no constructor of its own, `DinnerParty`'s automatic constructor calls `super()`, which matches `Party`'s no-argument version.

options.text: `int`
options.feedback: Nothing passes an `int` here. Java picks the parent constructor that matches the call, and `super()` has no arguments.

options.text: Nothing; a subclass with no constructor runs no constructors
options.feedback: Every object creation runs constructors. The subclass gets an automatic one, and it calls the parent's.

options.text: It does not compile; `DinnerParty` needs its own constructor
options.feedback: A subclass needs its own constructor only when every superclass constructor requires arguments. Here one doesn't.

questions.hint: Which superclass constructor does an automatic `super()` call match?
questions.explanation: If a superclass has a default (no-argument) constructor, its subclasses don't need constructors. A subclass without one gets Java's automatic constructor, which calls the superclass's default constructor.
questions.aside: Since Java 25, a constructor may run statements *before* its `super(...)` call, as long as they don't use the object being built: handy for checking an argument first. In Java 21 and earlier, `super(...)` must be the first statement.

questions.concept: Subclass constructor parameters can differ from the parent's
questions.stem: `DinnerPartyWithConstructor2` must call `PartyWithConstructor2(int numGuests)`. Which statement about its constructor is accurate?

options.text: It must pass the parent an `int`; its own parameters are up to you
options.feedback: It could take no parameters and pass a constant, or take several and pass one along. The only requirement is the call to `super`.

options.text: It must have exactly one `int` parameter, matching the parent
options.feedback: Matching is common but not required. `public DinnerPartyWithConstructor2() { super(0); }` is legal.

options.text: It must assign `guests` itself, because constructors aren't inherited
options.feedback: Constructors aren't inherited, but the parent's still runs through `super(...)`, and it sets `guests`. The child sets only its own fields.

options.text: It may take parameters only if it passes all of them to `super`
options.feedback: A subclass constructor can keep some arguments for its own fields, such as `dinnerChoice`, and pass the rest to its parent.

questions.hint: What exactly does the parent's constructor need from the child?
questions.explanation: When a superclass constructor requires arguments, the subclass constructor must call `super(...)` and give it what it needs. The subclass constructor's own parameter list is independent: it can supply constants, forward some parameters, or keep others for subclass fields.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.4, You Do It: Inheritance When the Superclass Requires Constructor Arguments (p. 343)

checks.title: Accessing Superclass Methods
checks.subtitle: Reusing an overridden method with super, and when this and super refer to different methods
checks.intro: A preferred customer's receipt needs everything a regular receipt shows, plus a discount line, and the regular version is already written. Four questions on reaching past your own override.
takeaways: Inside a subclass, `super.method()` runs the superclass version of a method even when the subclass overrides it. Unlike `super(...)` in a constructor, it can appear anywhere in the method.

When a subclass overrides a method, the plain name and `this.method()` both mean the subclass version; only `super.method()` reaches the parent's. When it doesn't override, all three reach the same inherited method.
An overriding method that calls its own name without `super.` calls itself, and with no way to stop, it recurses until a `StackOverflowError` ends the program.

questions.concept: super.method() reuses the parent's version
questions.stem: `PreferredCustomer` overrides `display()` and calls `super.display()` first. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `super.display()` runs `Customer`'s version, which prints the id and balance; then the child's own statement adds the rate.
This treats `super.display()` as reading some other, empty `Customer`. It runs on this same object, whose id and balance `super(id, bal)` already set.
This runs the parent's version on its own and then again inside the child's. Only the child's `display()` runs for the object, and it calls the parent's once.
The order follows the statements in the child's method, and `super.display()` comes first.

questions.hint: Trace the child's `display()` one statement at a time. What does its first statement run?
questions.explanation: When a subclass overrides a method but still wants the superclass behavior, it calls `super.methodName()`. The parent's version runs at that point, then the rest of the child's method continues.

questions.concept: this and super differ after an override
questions.stem: `ChildClass` overrides `someMethod()`. What does `new ChildClass().aDifferentMethod()` print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `C C P`
options.feedback: The plain name and `this.` both mean the child's own `someMethod()`. Only `super.` skips past the override to the parent's.

options.text: `C P P`
options.feedback: `this` refers to the current object, a `ChildClass`, so `this.someMethod()` runs the child's version, just like the plain call.

options.text: `P P P`
options.feedback: Inside the child, the override is in effect. Only the call through `super` gets the parent's version.

options.text: `C C C`
options.feedback: `super.someMethod()` always reaches the superclass version, even when the child overrides it.

questions.hint: Which object does `this` refer to, and where does `super` start looking?
questions.explanation: If a subclass overrides `someMethod()`, then within the subclass `someMethod()` and `this.someMethod()` refer to the subclass version, and `super.someMethod()` refers to the superclass version.

questions.concept: Without an override, all three reach the same method
questions.stem: `ChildClass2` does **not** override `someMethod()`. What does `new ChildClass2().aDifferentMethod()` print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `P P P`
options.feedback: The child has only the inherited method. The plain name, `this.` and `super.` all find that one `someMethod()`.

options.text: It does not compile: `this.someMethod()` needs a method declared in `ChildClass2`
options.feedback: An inherited method is a member of the subclass, so `this.someMethod()` finds it without the child declaring it.

options.text: It does not compile: `super` can only be used with an overridden method
options.feedback: `super.someMethod()` works whether or not the child overrides it. It's only *needed* when it does.

options.text: `P P` and then nothing, because `super` has nothing new to call
options.feedback: Every call runs the inherited method; `super.someMethod()` isn't skipped just because it runs the same code.

questions.hint: If the child declares no `someMethod()`, how many versions of it exist for a `ChildClass2` object?
questions.explanation: If a subclass has not overridden an inherited method, it can call that method with `super.`, with `this.` or with the name alone, because the superclass method is a member of the subclass by inheritance. All three run the same code.

questions.concept: Calling your own name instead of super recurses
questions.stem: A student meant to reuse the parent's `display()` but left out `super.`. What happens when `display()` is called on a `PreferredCustomer`?

code.label: Java

options.text: It throws a `StackOverflowError`
options.feedback: Inside the override, `display()` means the child's own method, so it calls itself again and again until the call stack runs out.

options.text: It prints the customer line, then the rate
options.feedback: That's what `super.display()` would do. Without `super.`, the call reaches the child's version, not `Customer`'s.

options.text: It does not compile, because a method can't call itself
options.feedback: Java allows a method to call itself (recursion). The compiler can't tell that this one never stops.

options.text: It prints `rate 0.15` once, because Java skips a call to the current method
options.feedback: Java never skips a call. The first statement calls `display()` again before the `print()` is ever reached.

questions.hint: Within `PreferredCustomer`, which version of `display()` does the plain name refer to?
questions.explanation: Within a subclass that overrides a method, the method's plain name means the subclass version. Calling it from inside that same method makes it call itself forever; only `super.methodName()` reaches the parent's version.
questions.aside: Each method call reserves a frame on the thread's call stack, and the stack has a fixed size, often 1 MB by default on 64-bit systems. Java's `-Xss` option changes it, but no size survives a recursion that never stops.

checks.title: Employing Information Hiding
checks.subtitle: Private members in subclasses, protected access, and why classes that reach into their parents are fragile
checks.intro: A new `PartTimeStudent` class wants to change its own ID number directly, and the compiler says no. Four questions on who may touch a parent's data.
takeaways: A subclass object contains its parent's private fields, but subclass methods can't name them. They reach that data through the parent's public methods, like any other class.
`protected` is the middle level: the class and its descendants can use the member directly, while outside classes can't. Use it sparingly.
Classes that use their parent's fields directly are fragile: a change inside the parent can break them, and they skip any rules the parent's methods enforce.

questions.concept: Subclass methods can't use the parent's private fields
questions.stem: What happens when `PartTimeStudent` is compiled?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `idNum` has private access in `Student`
options.feedback: Private members can be used only by methods of the class that declares them. Not even a subclass gets an exception.

options.text: It compiles, because a subclass inherits every field of its parent
options.feedback: It does inherit the field, which is in every `PartTimeStudent` object, but inheriting it doesn't grant access to it.

options.text: It compiles, but `idNum` is a new field unrelated to `Student`'s
options.feedback: Assigning to `idNum` doesn't declare anything. The compiler finds `Student`'s field and reports that it is private.

options.text: It compiles, then throws an exception when `resetId()` runs
options.feedback: Access rules are checked when the code is compiled, so the program never gets as far as running.

questions.hint: Who is allowed to use a member marked `private`?
questions.explanation: Subclasses inherit all of their superclass's data and methods, but private members of the parent are not accessible within the child class's methods. Otherwise any class could bypass information hiding just by extending another.

questions.concept: Private data is still reachable through public methods
questions.stem: This version of `PartTimeStudent` goes through `Student`'s public methods. What does the code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: The child object contains `Student`'s `idNum` field. `setIdNum()` stores 812 there, and `getIdNum()` reads it back.
This imagines the child having a separate copy that `setIdNum()` doesn't touch. There is one `idNum` in the object, and the setter changes it.

options.text: It does not compile, because `show()` reads a private field
options.feedback: `show()` never names `idNum`. It calls the public `getIdNum()`, which is allowed to read the private field.

options.text: It does not compile, because a subclass can't call its parent's setters
options.feedback: A subclass can call any nonprivate method it inherits; `setIdNum()` is public.

questions.hint: Which line names `idNum` directly, if any?
questions.explanation: A child class can work with its parent's private fields by using the public methods the parent defines, just as any other class can. The private field still exists in the child object; only direct access is blocked.

questions.concept: protected gives descendants direct access
questions.stem: `FullTimeStudent` and `PartTimeStudent` should use `gpa` directly, but a class like `Registrar`, which is unrelated and in another package, should **not**. Which declaration in `Student` fits?

options.text: `protected double gpa;`
options.feedback: `protected` members can be used by the class and its descendants, while unrelated outside classes are kept out.

options.text: `public double gpa;`
options.feedback: Public gives the subclasses access, but `Registrar` gets it too, which defeats information hiding.

options.text: `double gpa;` with no access specifier
options.feedback: Without a specifier, access is package-level: subclasses in a different package lose access.

options.text: `private static double gpa;`
options.feedback: `static` would make one `gpa` shared by every student, and `private` still locks the subclasses out.

questions.hint: You want an access level between `public` and `private`. Which keyword names it?
questions.explanation: `protected` provides an intermediate level of security between public and private: a protected field or method can be used within its own class and in any class extended from it, but not by unrelated outside classes.
questions.aside: Java's `protected` is a little more open than the name suggests: it also lets every class in the *same package* use the member. C# and C++ keep protected strictly to the class and its descendants.

questions.concept: Direct field access makes subclasses fragile
questions.stem: A teammate makes every `Student` field `protected` "so subclasses run faster." What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Subclasses then depend on `Student`'s internals and skip its validation
options.feedback: Children that use parent fields directly break when the parent changes, and they can store values the parent's setters would reject.

options.text: Protected fields can't be read by `Student`'s own methods
options.feedback: The class itself always has access to its own members, whatever their specifier.

options.text: Subclasses no longer inherit fields once they're protected
options.feedback: Protected fields are inherited and usable in subclasses; that's exactly what the teammate is counting on.

options.text: It's not faster at all: protected access is slower than calling a method
options.feedback: Direct access does avoid the method call, so it can be slightly faster. The objection is about safety, not speed.

questions.hint: If `Student` later renames `gpa` or adds a rule to `setGpa()`, what happens to classes that use `gpa` directly?
questions.explanation: Protected data can be convenient and slightly faster, but it should be used sparingly. Whenever possible, even child classes should go through public methods, because classes that use their parents' fields directly are fragile: they are easy to break.

checks.title: Methods You Cannot Override
checks.subtitle: static methods are hidden, not overridden; final methods; final classes
checks.intro: A legal-notice method must say exactly the same thing in every subclass. Five questions on the three kinds of methods a subclass can't override.
takeaways: A subclass can't override `static`, `final`, or `final`-class methods. A `final` class can't be extended at all.
A `static` method in a subclass with the same signature *hides* the parent's. The version that runs is chosen from the declared type at compile time, not from the object at run time.
A static method has no `this` object, so it can't use `super`; to reuse the parent's static method, call it with the class name, as in `BaseballPlayer.showOrigins()`.

questions.concept: final methods can't be overridden
questions.stem: What happens when `ProfessionalBasketballPlayer` is compiled?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error, because `displayMessage()` is final in the parent
options.feedback: `final` on a method means every subclass must use the parent's version. Declaring a replacement is an error.

options.text: It compiles, and the child's message replaces the parent's
options.feedback: That's normal overriding, which `final` exists to prevent.

options.text: It compiles, but the parent's message always runs instead
options.feedback: Java doesn't quietly ignore the child's method; the compiler refuses the class.

options.text: It compiles, because `@Override` lets a child replace a final method
options.feedback: `@Override` only checks that you are overriding. It can't unlock a `final` method.

questions.hint: What does `final` promise about a method's definition?
questions.explanation: A subclass cannot override a method declared `final` in its superclass. Use `final` when every child class must use the original parent version.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.7, A Subclass Cannot Override final Methods (pp. 350–351)

questions.concept: A final class can't be extended
questions.stem: `HideAndGoSeekPlayer` is declared `public final class`. Which statement about it is accurate?

options.text: No class can extend it, so none of its methods can ever be overridden
options.feedback: A final class can't be a parent at all, which makes every one of its methods effectively final.

options.text: Classes can extend it, but they can't add new fields
options.feedback: The restriction is stronger: `extends HideAndGoSeekPlayer` itself is a compile error.

options.text: Its fields become constants that can't change after construction
options.feedback: `final` on a class says nothing about its fields. A final class can have ordinary fields that change.

options.text: It can't be instantiated; it only provides methods to other classes
options.feedback: That describes an abstract class, the opposite case. A final class is meant to be used, not extended.

questions.hint: Can a final class appear after `extends` in another class header?
questions.explanation: When you declare a class `final`, all of its methods are final and the class cannot be a parent. Java's `Math` class is an example.
questions.aside: `java.lang.String` is final too. Because nobody can subclass it, code that receives a `String` can trust that it behaves like a real `String`, which matters when strings carry file names or passwords.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.7, A Subclass Cannot Override Methods in a final Superclass (pp. 351–352)

questions.concept: Reusing a parent's static method by class name
questions.stem: The child's static method hides the parent's and calls it by class name. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Doubleday 1871`
options.feedback: The child's static `showOrigins()` runs, and its first statement calls the parent's static version through the class name.
This misses the first statement. `BaseballPlayer.showOrigins()` explicitly runs the parent's method.

options.text: `Doubleday`
options.feedback: The child's method hides the parent's, so the call starts in the child's version, which prints both words.

options.text: It does not compile, because a static method can't call another class's method
options.feedback: Any class can call another class's nonprivate static method with the class name and a dot.

questions.hint: Which `showOrigins()` does the call on `aYankee` start in, and what does its first statement do?
questions.explanation: A subclass can hide a superclass static method by declaring one with the same signature. It can't use `super` there, but it can call the parent's nonprivate static method by class name, as any class can.

questions.concept: Hidden static methods follow the declared type
questions.stem: The variable is declared as the parent type but holds a child object. What does this print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Doubleday`
options.feedback: Static methods aren't overridden, so the call is bound from the declared type, `BaseballPlayer`, when the code is compiled.
That would be true for an instance method, which follows the object. Static methods follow the variable's declared type.

options.text: `Doubleday 1871`
options.feedback: Nothing calls both methods. One `showOrigins()` runs, and the declared type decides which.

options.text: It does not compile, because a static method can't be called with a variable
options.feedback: Java allows it (though it's misleading style); the compiler uses the variable's declared type to pick the method.

questions.hint: A static method belongs to a class, not an object. Which class does the compiler see for `player`?
questions.explanation: Instance methods use dynamic binding: the object's actual class decides at run time. Static methods use static binding: the declared type decides at compile time. That is why a subclass static method only hides, and never overrides, the parent's.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.7, A Subclass Cannot Override static Methods (p. 348); Ch. 9.9 (p. 360)

questions.concept: An instance method can't override a static one
questions.stem: A child class tries to replace a static method with an instance method. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: an instance method can't override a static method
options.feedback: A static method belongs to the class, so there is nothing per-object to override. The compiler rejects the attempt.

options.text: It compiles; objects use the child's version and the class uses the parent's
options.feedback: Java doesn't let one name be static in the parent and an instance method in the child; it refuses the class.

options.text: It compiles, but only after removing the `@Override` annotation
options.feedback: The annotation isn't the problem. Even without it, an instance method with this signature clashes with the static one.

options.text: It compiles, and `showOrigins()` becomes an instance method in both classes
options.feedback: A subclass can't change how its parent declares a method; `BaseballPlayer`'s version stays static.

questions.hint: Does a static method belong to an object or to a class?
questions.explanation: A subclass cannot override a static superclass method with an instance method; the compiler reports an error. The only legal same-signature method in the subclass is another static method, which hides the parent's.

checks.title: Creating and Using Abstract Classes
checks.subtitle: Abstract classes and methods, what concrete subclasses must provide, and abstract-class constructors
checks.intro: Every animal in a petting-zoo app makes a sound, but there's no such thing as a plain "animal" sound. Five questions on classes made only to be extended.
takeaways: An `abstract` class exists only to be extended; you can't instantiate it with `new`. It can still have fields, constructors and ordinary methods that its children inherit.
An abstract method has a header ending in a semicolon and no body. A class with an abstract method must itself be abstract.
A concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method; otherwise it must be declared abstract too.

questions.concept: Abstract classes can't be instantiated
questions.stem: `Animal` is declared `abstract`. What happens when this code is compiled?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `Animal` is abstract and can't be instantiated
options.feedback: An abstract class exists only to be extended. The compiler rejects any attempt to create one with `new`.

options.text: It compiles, then throws an exception when `new Animal()` runs
options.feedback: The compiler stops this before the program ever runs, because it can see the class is abstract.

options.text: It compiles; Java creates a plain `Animal` with no `speak()` behavior
options.feedback: There is no such thing as a plain `Animal` object; preventing that is the point of `abstract`.

options.text: It compiles, because `Animal` has a concrete `setName()` method
options.feedback: One abstract method is enough to make the class unfinished, and `abstract` on the class forbids `new` regardless.

questions.hint: What does declaring a class `abstract` say about creating objects of it?
questions.explanation: A concrete class is one you can instantiate; an abstract class is one you create only to extend. Any attempt to create an object of an abstract class with `new` fails to compile.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.8, Creating and Using Abstract Classes (pp. 352–354)

questions.concept: Concrete subclasses must implement abstract methods
questions.stem: `Cow` extends the abstract `Animal` but forgets `speak()`. What happens when `Cow` is compiled?

code.label: Java

error_contains: does not override abstract method speak()

options.text: A compile error: `Cow` doesn't override the abstract `speak()`
options.feedback: A concrete subclass inherits the obligation. It must give `speak()` a body or be declared abstract itself.

options.text: It compiles, and `Cow` inherits an empty `speak()` that does nothing
options.feedback: An abstract method has no body to inherit, empty or otherwise. That's why the subclass must provide one.

options.text: It compiles, and calling `speak()` on a `Cow` throws an exception
options.feedback: The compiler catches the missing method, so no `Cow` object can be created to call it.

options.text: It compiles, because `Cow` adds no fields that would need `speak()`
options.feedback: The requirement doesn't depend on fields. Every inherited abstract method must be implemented.

questions.hint: Which methods must a class implement before you can create objects from it?
questions.explanation: When a class inherits an abstract method, it must either provide a body for it or be declared abstract itself. A concrete subclass that skips one doesn't compile.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.8, Creating and Using Abstract Classes (p. 353)

questions.concept: An abstract method requires an abstract class
questions.stem: A student declares an abstract method in a class that isn't marked `abstract`. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: a class with an abstract method must be abstract
options.feedback: An abstract method leaves the class unfinished, so the class can't be concrete. Adding `abstract` to the header fixes it.

options.text: It compiles, and `Vehicle` becomes abstract automatically
options.feedback: Java doesn't change your declarations for you; it reports the mismatch.

options.text: It compiles; `setPrice()` is treated as an empty method
options.feedback: An abstract method has no body at all, and Java doesn't invent one.

options.text: It compiles, because only interfaces may not hold abstract methods
options.feedback: Interfaces are full of abstract methods. The problem is a concrete class declaring one.

questions.hint: Could you create a `Vehicle` object and call `setPrice()` on it? What would run?
questions.explanation: If you declare a method abstract, you must also declare its class abstract. In an abstract class, each method can be abstract or not.

questions.concept: Abstract classes have constructors that run
questions.stem: An abstract class can't be instantiated. Can its constructor ever run? What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Vehicle Sailboat`
options.feedback: Creating a `Sailboat` runs its parent's constructor first. The abstract parent's constructor builds its part of the object.

options.text: `Sailboat`
options.feedback: This assumes an abstract class's constructor never runs. It runs every time a subclass object is created.

options.text: `Sailboat Vehicle`
options.feedback: Constructors run from the most general class down, so `Vehicle` prints before `Sailboat`.

options.text: It does not compile, because an abstract class can't declare a constructor
options.feedback: Abstract classes can and often do have constructors; you just can't call them with `new` directly.

questions.hint: When a `Sailboat` object is created, which constructor runs first?
questions.explanation: An abstract class can declare fields and constructors. Its constructor is invoked whenever a child class object is instantiated, usually through the child's `super(...)` call.
questions.aside: Java's own `Number` class is abstract. You never create a plain `Number`, but `Integer`, `Double` and `Long` all extend it, and its constructor runs every time one of them is created.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.8, You Do It: Creating an Abstract Class (pp. 355–357); Table 9-3 (p. 373)

questions.concept: Each subclass supplies its own body
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Murphy says Woof! Elsie says Moo!`
options.feedback: Both objects inherit `setName()` and `getName()` from `Animal`, and each runs its own class's `speak()`.

options.text: `Murphy says Woof! Elsie says Woof!`
options.feedback: Each subclass implements `speak()` independently; `Cow`'s version doesn't borrow `Dog`'s.

options.text: `null says Woof! null says Moo!`
options.feedback: `setName()` stores each name in that object's inherited `name` field before `getName()` reads it.

options.text: `says Woof! says Moo!`
options.feedback: `getName()` is inherited from the abstract class and returns the name each object stored.

questions.hint: Which methods does each animal inherit from `Animal`, and which does it supply itself?
questions.explanation: An abstract class can supply concrete methods, such as `getName()`, that every child inherits, while abstract methods, such as `speak()`, force each child to supply its own behavior. One method name causing different, appropriate actions is polymorphism.

checks.title: Using Dynamic Method Binding
checks.subtitle: Superclass references to subclass objects, choosing the method at run time, and superclass parameters
checks.intro: One method, `talkingAnimal()`, has to work for dogs, cows and every animal class nobody has written yet. Five questions on how Java picks the right `speak()`.
takeaways: A superclass reference can hold any subclass object (every `Dog` is an `Animal`), but a subclass reference can't hold a superclass object.
For an instance method, the object's actual class picks the version that runs, and it is chosen while the program runs. This is dynamic (late) method binding.
The compiler, though, checks calls against the variable's *declared* type: through an `Animal` reference you can call only methods `Animal` declares, even when the object is a `Dog`.

questions.concept: The object, not the variable, picks the method
questions.stem: One `Animal` variable refers first to a `Cow`, then to a `Dog`. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Moo! Woof!`
options.feedback: The same statement, `animalRef.speak()`, runs whichever version belongs to the object the variable holds at that moment.

options.text: It does not compile, because `Animal` is abstract
options.feedback: You can't create an `Animal` object, but you can declare an `Animal` *reference* and store concrete subclass objects in it.

options.text: `Woof! Woof!`
options.feedback: Each call happens when the variable holds a different object; the first one holds the `Cow`.

options.text: `Moo! Moo!`
options.feedback: Assigning `new Dog()` replaces what the variable refers to, so the second call reaches `Dog`'s `speak()`.

questions.hint: At the moment of each `speak()` call, which object does `animalRef` refer to?
questions.explanation: A superclass reference can hold any subclass object. When you call an instance method through it, Java runs the version for the object's actual class, so one statement can produce different behavior.

questions.concept: Child objects fit parent references, not the reverse
questions.stem: `Employee` is a concrete class and `SalariedEmployee` extends it. Which statement compiles?

options.text: `Employee worker = new SalariedEmployee();`
options.feedback: Every `SalariedEmployee` is an `Employee`, so a parent reference can hold a child object. This is upcasting.

options.text: `SalariedEmployee worker = new Employee();`
options.feedback: A plain `Employee` isn't a `SalariedEmployee`; it lacks whatever the subclass adds, so the compiler refuses.

options.text: `SalariedEmployee worker = (Employee) new SalariedEmployee();`
options.feedback: The cast makes the right side an `Employee`, and an `Employee` can't be stored in a `SalariedEmployee` variable without a cast the other way.

options.text: `Employee worker = SalariedEmployee();`
options.feedback: Without `new`, Java reads this as a call to a method named `SalariedEmployee()`, which doesn't exist.

questions.hint: Complete the sentence for each: "Every ___ is an ___." Which way is always true?
questions.explanation: Because every subclass object is a superclass object, you can assign a subclass object to a superclass reference (upcasting). You can't assign a superclass object to a subclass reference.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.9, Using Dynamic Method Binding (p. 359); Two Truths & a Lie (p. 361)

questions.concept: The compiler checks the declared type
questions.stem: Only `Dog` declares `fetch()`. The object really is a `Dog`. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `Animal` has no `fetch()` method
options.feedback: The compiler knows only the variable's type, `Animal`, and checks the call against it. Which object it will hold is a run-time fact.

options.text: It prints `Fetching!`, because the object is a `Dog`
options.feedback: The object's class matters when Java chooses among *existing* versions of a method. First the call must be legal for `Animal`.

options.text: It compiles, then throws an exception because `Animal` lacks `fetch()`
options.feedback: The check happens at compile time, so the program never runs.

options.text: It prints nothing; Java skips methods the reference type can't see
options.feedback: Java never silently skips a call. It reports the problem at compile time.

questions.hint: When the compiler reads `pet.fetch()`, what does it know about `pet`?
questions.explanation: Dynamic binding chooses *which version* of a method runs, based on the object. Whether a call is allowed at all is decided at compile time from the reference's declared type, so a superclass reference reaches only the methods the superclass declares.

questions.concept: Dynamic binding happens at run time
questions.stem: In `talkingAnimal(Animal animal)`, the statement `animal.speak();` is compiled once. When and how is the `speak()` version chosen?

options.text: While the program runs, from the actual class of the object passed in
options.feedback: The compiler can't know which `Animal` subclass will arrive; Java binds the call when it executes. That is dynamic, or late, binding.

options.text: When it compiles, from the parameter's declared type, `Animal`
options.feedback: That's static binding, which Java uses for static methods. Instance methods are virtual by default.

options.text: When it compiles, from the argument types in the calls in `main()`
options.feedback: The method is compiled independently of its callers, and later code could pass animal classes that didn't exist yet.

options.text: While the program runs, always using the first subclass that was loaded
options.feedback: The choice is made fresh for each call, from that call's object, so a `Dog` and then a `Cow` behave differently.

questions.hint: Could `talkingAnimal()` work with a `Horse` class written next year? How would Java know which `speak()` to run?
questions.explanation: Java instance method calls are virtual by default: the method used is determined when the program runs, from the object's type. Dynamic binding makes programs flexible, while static binding (used for class methods) is slightly faster.
questions.aside: Java and C++ made opposite choices. In C++ (and C#), a method is bound statically unless it is marked `virtual`. In Java, instance methods are virtual by default, and you opt out with `final`.

questions.concept: A superclass parameter accepts any subclass
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Ginger: Woof! Molly: Moo!`
options.feedback: Each call passes a different subclass object into the `Animal` parameter, and `speak()` runs that object's own version.

options.text: It does not compile: `talkingAnimal()` needs an `Animal`, not a `Dog`
options.feedback: A `Dog` is an `Animal`, so it can be passed wherever an `Animal` is expected. That is the payoff of upcasting.

options.text: `Ginger: Woof! Molly: Woof!`
options.feedback: The method doesn't remember the first object's class; every call binds `speak()` to the object it receives.

options.text: It does not compile, because an abstract class can't be a parameter type
options.feedback: Abstract classes can't be instantiated, but they are ideal parameter types; any concrete subclass object can be passed.

questions.hint: What is every `Dog` and every `Cow`, as far as the parameter type is concerned?
questions.explanation: A method whose parameter is a superclass type accepts objects of every subclass. Inside, dynamic binding makes overridden methods behave correctly for each argument, so one method serves every present and future subclass.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.9, Using a Superclass as a Method Parameter Type (pp. 360–361)

checks.title: Creating Arrays of Subclass Objects
checks.subtitle: Arrays of superclass references, filling them with subclass objects, and looping over them polymorphically
checks.intro: A vehicle dealer's inventory mixes sailboats and bicycles, and one loop has to describe them all. Four questions on arrays that hold a whole family of classes.
takeaways: An array of objects is really an array of references. `new Animal[3]` creates three empty (`null`) references and no `Animal` objects, which is why it works even when `Animal` is abstract.
An array of superclass references can hold any mix of subclass objects; looping over it and calling an overridden method runs each object's own version.
Every element must be filled before you call a method through it: calling a method on a `null` element throws a `NullPointerException`.

questions.concept: One loop, each object's own method
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Woof! Moo! Ssss!`
options.feedback: The array holds `Animal` references to three different subclass objects, and each `speak()` call is bound to its own object.

options.text: It does not compile, because the array's type is abstract

options.text: `Ssss! Moo! Woof!`

options.text: `Woof! Woof! Woof!`
options.feedback: Each element refers to a different object; the first element's class doesn't decide the others.

questions.hint: What kind of object does each element refer to when the loop reaches it?
questions.explanation: An array of superclass references can hold references to any subclass objects. Looping over it and calling an overridden method invokes the appropriate version for each element.

questions.concept: An array of objects is an array of references

options.text: Three `Animal` references, each `null`, and no `Animal` objects

questions.hint: What sits in each slot of a newly created array of a class type?
questions.explanation: When you create an array of a class type, you are not constructing objects; you are creating space for references. This works whether the class is abstract or concrete, and each element is `null` until you assign an object to it.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.10, Creating Arrays of Subclass Objects (p. 361)

questions.stem: The programmer filled only the first element. What happens when this code runs?

code.label: Java

options.text: It prints `Woof!` and then throws a `NullPointerException`

questions.explanation: Each element of a new object array is `null` until you assign an object. Calling a method through a `null` reference throws a `NullPointerException` at run time.
questions.aside: Tony Hoare, who added null references to the ALGOL W language in 1965, later called them his "billion-dollar mistake" because of the crashes they have caused ever since.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.10, Creating Arrays of Subclass Objects (p. 361)
