checks.title: Using the Object Class and Its Methods
checks.subtitle: Every class extends Object; toString(); equals() by reference, overloaded and overridden; hashCode()
checks.intro: Two bank accounts with the same number and balance, and Java says they're not equal. Six questions on the methods every class gets for free, and when to replace them.
takeaways: Every class that doesn't extend another implicitly extends `Object`, so every object has `toString()`, `equals()` and `hashCode()`. The inherited versions are generic: the class name and a hash code, and equal only to itself.

To compare objects by their contents, write your own `equals()`. Overriding needs the exact header `public boolean equals(Object obj)`; a version with a narrower parameter type only overloads and is skipped when the argument's declared type is `Object`.

A robust `equals(Object)` returns true for the same object, false for `null` or a different class, and only then casts and compares fields. Whenever you override `equals()`, override `hashCode()` too, so equal objects have equal hash codes.

questions.concept: Object's equals() compares references
questions.stem: `BankAccount` doesn't define `equals()`. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `not equal`
options.feedback: The inherited `Object` version returns `true` only when both references point to the same object, and these are two separate objects.

options.text: `equal`
options.feedback: Matching field values don't matter to the inherited method; it never looks at fields.

options.text: It does not compile, because `BankAccount` has no `equals()` method
options.feedback: Every class inherits `equals()` from `Object`, so the call compiles.

options.text: It throws an exception, because `equals()` must be overridden first
options.feedback: `Object`'s `equals()` is a normal, working method, not an abstract one; it runs and returns a result.

questions.hint: Where does `acct1.equals()` come from, and what does that version compare?
questions.explanation: Every class extends `Object`, which supplies `equals()`. That version considers two references equal only when they refer to the same object, so two separately created objects with identical data are not equal unless you write your own `equals()`.

questions.concept: The inherited toString()
questions.stem: Neither `Dog` nor `Animal` defines `toString()`. What does `System.out.println(myDog.toString());` display?

code.label: Java

options.text: The class name, `@`, and a hexadecimal hash code, such as `Dog@5679c6c6`
options.feedback: `Dog` inherits `toString()` from `Object`, whose version reports the class name and the object's hash code.

options.text: Nothing; the call doesn't compile, because no class here defines `toString()`
options.feedback: `Dog` doesn't need to define it: every class inherits `toString()` from `Object`.

options.text: The values of the object's fields, such as `name=Murphy`
options.feedback: `Object` can't know which fields matter to your class. For a field listing, you write your own `toString()`.

options.text: The variable's name, `myDog`, followed by its class name
options.feedback: Objects don't know the names of the variables that refer to them; many variables can refer to one object.

questions.hint: Which class provides `toString()` to every other class, and what can that class know about your fields?
questions.explanation: Every class inherits `toString()` from `Object`. The inherited version returns the class name, an `@` sign and a hexadecimal hash code, which is rarely useful; it's usually better to write your own `toString()` that shows the object's field values.

questions.concept: toString() as a debugging tool
questions.stem: This `BankAccount` has a bug. What does the program print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `BankAccount 123 Balance $123.0`
options.feedback: The constructor stores the account number in both fields, and `toString()` makes the mistake visible at a glance.

options.text: `BankAccount 123 Balance $4567.89`
options.feedback: That's what the programmer meant. Look at what the constructor actually assigns to `balance`.

options.text: `BankAccount 123 Balance $123`
options.feedback: `balance` is a `double`, so even a whole number prints with a decimal point: `123.0`.

options.text: `BankAccount 123 Balance $0.0`
options.feedback: The constructor does assign `balance`; it just assigns the wrong parameter.

questions.hint: Which parameter does the constructor store in `balance`?
questions.explanation: Overriding `toString()` to show an object's fields is a quick way to inspect its state while debugging. Because `toString()` comes from `Object`, it is the conventional name programmers look for.

questions.concept: An overloaded equals() is skipped for Object arguments
questions.stem: `BankAccount` *overloads* `equals()` with a `BankAccount` parameter. The second call passes the same object through an `Object` variable. What does this print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `true false`
options.feedback: The compiler picks an overload from declared types. `other` is declared `Object`, so the second call uses `Object`'s inherited version, which compares references.

options.text: `true true`
options.feedback: That would happen if the method *overrode* `equals(Object)`. An overload is chosen only when the argument's declared type is `BankAccount`.

options.text: `false false`
options.feedback: The first call's argument is declared `BankAccount`, so it reaches the new method, which compares fields and finds them equal.

options.text: It does not compile, because `equals(Object)` and `equals(BankAccount)` clash
options.feedback: Different parameter lists make them legal overloads; the class has access to both.

questions.hint: The object is the same in both calls. What differs between the two arguments, as the compiler sees them?
questions.explanation: A method with the header `equals(BankAccount)` overloads `Object`'s `equals(Object)` rather than overriding it. Overloads are chosen at compile time from declared argument types, so whenever the argument is declared `Object`, the inherited reference comparison runs. Overriding requires the exact `equals(Object)` signature.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.11, Overloading equals() and Overriding equals() (pp. 367–369)

questions.concept: A robust equals() handles null before casting
questions.stem: A teammate overrides `equals()` following some of the recommendations. What happens when `acct1.equals(null)` runs?

code.label: Java

options.text: It throws a `NullPointerException`
options.feedback: The `null` test sets `result`, but nothing stops the method there. It goes on to cast `null` and read `secondAcct.acctNum`, which fails.

options.text: It returns `false`, because the `null` test sets `result` to `false`
options.feedback: Setting `result` doesn't end the method. The statements after the `if` chain still run, and the last `if` overwrites `result`.

options.text: It returns `true`, because the method reaches its last `if` and compares fields
options.feedback: It does reach the last `if`, but reading `secondAcct.acctNum` through `null` fails before any comparison is made.

options.text: It does not compile, because `null` can't be passed as an `Object`
options.feedback: `null` can be passed for any reference parameter. The trouble is what the method does with it.

questions.hint: Follow the method for `obj == null`. Does anything stop it from reaching the cast and the field reads?
questions.explanation: A robust `equals(Object)` returns `true` for the same object and `false` for `null` or an object of a different class, and only then casts and compares fields. Setting a result variable isn't enough; the method must return before the cast, or put the cast inside an `else`.

questions.concept: Override hashCode() with equals()
questions.stem: Java's creators recommend overriding `hashCode()` whenever you override `equals()`. Why?

options.text: Equal objects must have equal hash codes, or hash-based code misbehaves
options.feedback: Hash-based collections use the hash code to decide where to look. Two equal accounts with different codes are treated as different.

options.text: The compiler rejects a class that overrides only one of the two
options.feedback: The compiler accepts it; the problem shows up later, as wrong results in programs that rely on hash codes.

options.text: `Object`'s `equals()` calls `hashCode()`, so the old one breaks the new `equals()`
options.feedback: `Object`'s `equals()` compares references directly; your override doesn't depend on `hashCode()` at all.

options.text: `toString()` uses `hashCode()`, so overriding it gives readable output
options.feedback: The default `toString()` does show a hash code, but readable output comes from overriding `toString()` itself.

questions.hint: If two accounts are `equals()`, what should be true of their hash codes?
questions.explanation: The default hash code is tied to the object's identity, so two objects your `equals()` calls equal would usually get different codes. Programs that use hash-based methods then treat equal objects as different, so override `hashCode()` from the same fields `equals()` compares.
questions.aside: Since Java 7, `java.util.Objects.hash(acctNum, balance)` builds a reasonable hash code from any list of fields in one line, so you don't have to hand-pick prime multipliers.

checks.title: Creating and Using Interfaces
checks.subtitle: Why Java has no multiple inheritance, implementing interfaces, interface constants, and abstract class or interface?
checks.intro: A rental company's `InsuredAutomobile` is both an insured item and an automobile, but a Java class gets only one parent. Five questions on the alternative.
takeaways: Java forbids multiple inheritance: a class `extends` at most one class. It can `implement` any number of interfaces, which list method headers without saying how they work.

A class that implements an interface must provide every one of its abstract methods, as `public` methods, or be declared abstract. Interface data fields are always `public`, `static` and `final` constants.

Choose an abstract class when subclasses should inherit shared code or data; choose an interface when unrelated classes must each supply their own version of the same behavior, or when a class needs behavior from more than one source.

questions.concept: One superclass, any number of interfaces
questions.stem: `Dog` is a class and `Worker` is an interface. Which class header compiles?

options.text: `public class WorkingDog extends Dog implements Worker`
options.feedback: One superclass after `extends`, then interfaces after `implements`, in that order.

options.text: `public class WorkingDog extends Dog, Worker`
options.feedback: A class can extend only one class, and an interface is added with `implements`, not `extends`.

options.text: `public class WorkingDog implements Worker extends Dog`
options.feedback: Both keywords belong in the header, but the `extends` clause must come first.

options.text: `public class WorkingDog implements Dog, Worker`
options.feedback: `implements` lists interfaces only. `Dog` is a class, so it must follow `extends`.

questions.hint: Which keyword introduces a class's single parent, and which introduces interfaces?
questions.explanation: Java prohibits inheriting directly from two classes. A class names one superclass with `extends` and any number of interfaces with `implements`, and the `implements` clause follows the `extends` clause.

questions.concept: Implementing methods must be public
questions.stem: `WorkingDog` implements `work()` but leaves off `public`. What happens when it compiles?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `work()` would have weaker access than in `Worker`
options.feedback: Interface methods are implicitly public, and an implementing method can't be less visible. Without `public`, it has package access.

options.text: It compiles, because the interface's `public` carries over automatically
options.feedback: "Implicitly public" applies inside the interface, not to the class that implements it. In a class, no specifier means package access.

options.text: It compiles, but `work()` can be called only from inside `WorkingDog`
options.feedback: That would be `private` access. Either way, the compiler won't accept a narrower method.

options.text: It compiles, because `WorkingDog` also inherits public methods from `Dog`
options.feedback: What `Dog` provides doesn't change the rule for `work()`, which must match the interface's public access.

questions.hint: In the interface, `work()` is public. In this class, what access does a method with no specifier have?
questions.explanation: All methods in an interface are implicitly `public`. A class that implements one must declare each method `public` as well, because an overriding or implementing method can't reduce access.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.12, Creating and Using Interfaces (p. 371); Figure 9-57 (p. 372)

questions.concept: Interface fields are constants
questions.stem: `PizzaDemo` implements `PizzaConstants` and tries to raise the tax rate. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `TAX_RATE` is final and can't be assigned
options.feedback: Interface fields are `public static final` constants. Implementing classes can read them but never change them.

options.text: It prints `0.08`, because `PizzaDemo` gets its own copy of `TAX_RATE`
options.feedback: An interface field is `static`, so there is one shared constant, and it is `final`, so no class can reassign it.

options.text: It prints `0.07`, because the assignment is quietly ignored
options.feedback: Java doesn't ignore assignments to constants; the compiler reports them.

options.text: A compile error: `PizzaDemo` can't use `TAX_RATE` without a prefix
options.feedback: Implementing `PizzaConstants` lets the class use its constants by their simple names. The problem is the assignment.

questions.hint: What three modifiers does every interface field have, whether or not they are written?
questions.explanation: Interfaces can contain data fields, but they must be `public`, `static` and `final`. They are useful for a set of constants many classes share; implementing classes can use the values without redeclaring them, but can't change them.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.12, Creating Interfaces to Store Related Constants (pp. 374–375)

questions.concept: Choosing an abstract class or an interface
questions.stem: In a `CardGame` family, `shuffle()` works identically in every game, while `deal()` and `keepScore()` differ in each one. Which design fits best?

options.text: An abstract class with a complete `shuffle()` and abstract `deal()` and `keepScore()`
options.feedback: Every game inherits the one tested `shuffle()`, and each subclass is forced to write its own `deal()` and `keepScore()`.

options.text: An interface declaring all three methods, so each game writes its own `shuffle()`
options.feedback: It works, but every game would duplicate identical shuffling code. Shared behavior belongs where it can be inherited.

options.text: A final class with all three methods, so no game can change them
options.feedback: A final class can't be extended at all, so no game could supply its own `deal()` or `keepScore()`.

options.text: A concrete class with empty `deal()` and `keepScore()` methods to fill in later
options.feedback: Empty concrete methods compile, but nothing forces a subclass to replace them, so a game could silently do nothing.

questions.hint: Which method should be written once and inherited, and which ones must every game be forced to write?
questions.explanation: Create an abstract class when subclasses should inherit some data or working methods while being required to supply others. Create an interface when you know which actions every class needs but each class must define all of the behavior itself, or when a class needs behavior from more than one parent.
questions.aside: Since Java 8, an interface can also contain `default` methods with bodies, so interfaces can now share some code too. Abstract classes still offer what interfaces can't: instance fields and constructors.

questions.concept: An implementing class is-a its interface
questions.stem: `WorkingDog`'s `work()` calls the `speak()` it inherits from `Dog`. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Woof! Woof! I work 40 hours`
options.feedback: `speak()` runs once on its own, then `work()` runs `speak()` again before its own line.

options.text: `Woof! I work 40 hours`
options.feedback: This skips the separate `speak()` call in `main()`, which runs before `work()`.

options.text: `I work 40 hours`
options.feedback: `work()` begins by calling `speak()`, which `WorkingDog` inherits from `Dog`.

options.text: It does not compile: `work()` can't call `speak()`, which `Worker` lacks
options.feedback: `work()` is a method of `WorkingDog`, which inherits `speak()` from `Dog`. The interface only requires that `work()` exist.

questions.hint: List every call to `speak()`, including the one inside `work()`.
questions.explanation: A class that both extends a class and implements an interface can use its inherited methods and must supply the interface's methods. Like inheritance, implementing an interface creates an is-a relationship: a `WorkingDog` is a `Dog`, an `Animal` and a `Worker`.

checks.title: Using records, Anonymous Inner Classes, and Lambda Expressions
checks.subtitle: What a record generates, one-off classes with no name, effectively final variables, and functional interfaces
checks.intro: A class with two fields shouldn't need twenty lines of boilerplate, and a washing machine that works once shouldn't need its own file. Six questions on Java's shortcuts.
takeaways: A `record` declares only its components; Java generates private final fields, a constructor, accessors named after the components (no `get` prefix), and `equals()`, `hashCode()` and `toString()` based on the values.

An anonymous inner class creates a one-time object that extends a class or implements an interface, without naming the class, and without writing `extends` or `implements`. Local variables it uses must be final or effectively final.
A lambda expression such as `() -> { ... }` implements a functional interface, one with exactly one abstract method. If an interface has two abstract methods, a lambda can't implement it.

questions.concept: A record's generated toString()
questions.stem: `Building` is a record. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Building[address=47 Oak Street, squareFeet=600]`
options.feedback: A record's generated `toString()` lists the record name and each component's name and value in square brackets.

options.text: `Building[String address=47 Oak Street, int squareFeet=600]`
options.feedback: The record's header lists each component's type, but the generated `toString()` shows only names and values.

options.text: `address=47 Oak Street, squareFeet=600`
options.feedback: The generated version also names the record type, `Building`, and wraps the components in square brackets.

options.text: `Building(address=47 Oak Street, squareFeet=600)`
options.feedback: Close, but a record's `toString()` uses square brackets around the components, not parentheses.

questions.hint: Which methods does Java write for you when you declare a record?
questions.explanation: Every record automatically receives a private final field for each component, a public constructor, a public accessor for each component, and implementations of `equals()`, `hashCode()` and `toString()` that use the components' values.

questions.concept: Record accessors have no get prefix
questions.stem: A student uses the getter name they're used to. What happens when this compiles?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `Building` has no `getAddress()` method
options.feedback: A record's accessors are named exactly like its components, so the method is `address()`.

options.text: It prints `47 Oak Street`, because records generate `get` methods
options.feedback: Records do generate accessors, but without the `get` prefix: `bldg.address()`.

options.text: It prints `null`, because the record has no setter to store the address
options.feedback: The generated constructor stores the address. The problem is only the method's name.

options.text: A compile error: records can't be printed without a `toString()`
options.feedback: Records generate `toString()`; printing one is fine. The compiler objects to `getAddress()`.

questions.hint: In `TestBuildingRecord`, how did the book read the address back out?
questions.explanation: Each automatically generated record accessor is public and has the same name and type as its component, with no `get` prefix. Records also have no setters, because their fields are final.

questions.concept: Records compare by value
questions.stem: Two separately created `Building` objects hold the same values. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `false true`
options.feedback: `==` asks whether they are the same object, and they aren't. The record's generated `equals()` compares component values, which match.

options.text: `false false`
options.feedback: That's how a plain class without its own `equals()` behaves. A record generates a value-based `equals()`.

options.text: `true true`
options.feedback: `new` always creates a distinct object, so `==` on two `new` objects is false.

options.text: `true false`
options.feedback: This reverses the two tests: `==` compares references, while `equals()` here compares values.

questions.hint: Which of the two tests compares references, and which uses a method the record generated?
questions.explanation: Records generate `equals()` and `hashCode()` from their component values, so two records with the same data are equal. The `==` operator still compares references, and two `new` objects are always different references.
questions.aside: Records arrived as a preview in Java 14 and became a standard feature in Java 16, in 2021. Java 21 added record patterns, which unpack a record's components right inside an `instanceof` test or a `switch`.
questions.ref: Ch. 9.13, Using records (p. 379); Ch. 9.11, Using the equals() Method

questions.concept: An anonymous inner class extends or implements without saying so
questions.stem: The program creates a one-off `Animal` without naming its class. What does it print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Kiwi says Tweet!`
options.feedback: `new Animal() { ... }` defines an unnamed subclass of `Animal`, overrides `speak()` and creates one object of it, which inherits `setName()` and `getName()`.

options.text: It does not compile, because `Animal` is abstract
options.feedback: `new Animal()` alone would fail, but the braces that follow define a concrete, unnamed subclass that implements `speak()`.

options.text: It does not compile, because the class body needs `extends Animal`
options.feedback: An anonymous class never uses `extends` or `implements`; the type after `new` says what it extends or implements.

options.text: `null says Tweet!`
options.feedback: The unnamed subclass inherits `setName()`, which stores `"Kiwi"` before `getName()` reads it.

questions.hint: What do the curly braces right after `new Animal()` define?
questions.explanation: An anonymous inner class has no name and is defined where it is instantiated, with `new`. It either extends a class or implements an interface, without the keywords `extends` or `implements`, and it must override all inherited abstract methods.

questions.concept: Captured variables must be effectively final
questions.stem: The anonymous class uses `pounds`, and `pounds` is changed afterward. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `pounds` must be final or effectively final
options.feedback: `pounds` is assigned twice, so it isn't effectively final, and an inner class may use only local variables that never change.

options.text: It prints `25 pounds`, the value at the time `work()` is called
options.feedback: Java won't let the inner class see a variable that changes, precisely so this question never comes up at run time.

options.text: It prints `20 pounds`, the value when the object was created
options.feedback: That's how Java copies the value, but it allows the copy only when the variable can never change afterward.

options.text: It compiles, because the reassignment comes after the class definition
options.feedback: The rule looks at the whole method: a variable assigned more than once isn't effectively final, wherever the second assignment is.

questions.hint: How many times is `pounds` assigned in `main()`?
questions.explanation: An anonymous inner class can use local variables of its enclosing method only if they are final or effectively final, meaning assigned only once. The same rule applies to lambda expressions.

questions.concept: Lambdas need a functional interface
questions.stem: `Insured` declares two abstract methods. A student tries to implement it with a lambda. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: A compile error: `Insured` is not a functional interface
options.feedback: A lambda supplies exactly one method body, so it can implement only an interface with a single abstract method.

options.text: It compiles; the lambda implements both methods with the same body
options.feedback: One body can't serve both `void setCoverage()` and `int getCoverage()`. Java needs exactly one abstract method to match.

options.text: It compiles; the lambda implements `setCoverage()`, the first method
options.feedback: Java never guesses which method you meant. With two abstract methods, the interface can't be the target of a lambda.

options.text: It compiles, but calling `getCoverage()` throws an exception
options.feedback: The compiler rejects the lambda before anything can be called.

questions.hint: How many abstract methods may an interface have for a lambda to implement it?
questions.explanation: A lambda expression creates an object that implements a functional interface, an interface with exactly one abstract method. Because the interface has only one method, the lambda knows which method its body implements; with two abstract methods, a lambda can't be used, so you write a class or an anonymous class instead.
questions.aside: The name comes from lambda calculus, Alonzo Church's 1930s system for describing computation with functions alone, which writes a function with the Greek letter λ. Java added lambda expressions in Java 8, in 2014.
